normalize: normalize(x): recursive. Strings: CRLF/CR -> LF; U+00A0 -> space; rtrim each line; trim. Lists/maps: same order, values normalized.
reduce: reduce(stored) = for each stored item, q = trim(item.question ?? item.q ?? ""), a = trim(item.answer ?? item.a ?? ""); drop items where q or a is empty (faqPageSchema skips them); emit {question: q, answer: strip_tags(a)}. This is exactly the JSON-LD the live page emits.
op: Per slug: (1) if normalize(reduce(stored)) === normalize(new_faqs) -> skip "already at target". (2) elif normalize(reduce(stored)) !== normalize(old_faqs_guard) -> WARNING "old mismatch" + 200-char excerpt, write nothing. (3) else build the write value from the STORED array: same items in the same order; for each index in replace_indices, replace that stored item with new_faqs[index] (keys question/answer); every other stored item is kept byte-for-byte (C items stay exactly as stored, including any HTML). Assert normalize(reduce(result)) === normalize(new_faqs) before saveQuietly(); otherwise throw (rolls back the slug). If the stored array contains items dropped by reduce() (empty q/a), keep them in place and report the count. replace_indices refer to positions in reduce(stored); map them back to stored positions.

old_faqs_guard.question: Why is kisspeptin important for fertility?
old_faqs_guard.answer: Kisspeptin is the master upstream regulator of GnRH neurons, triggering the entire reproductive hormone cascade.

old_faqs_guard.question: Why does continuous kisspeptin cause tachyphylaxis?
old_faqs_guard.answer: Continuous exposure causes KISS1R receptor desensitization, paradoxically suppressing hormones. Pulsed dosing is essential.

old_faqs_guard.question: Do effects differ between men and women?
old_faqs_guard.answer: Yes. Men show robust LH stimulation at all times, but in women the response depends on menstrual cycle phase, strongest in the preovulatory period.

new_faqs.question: Why is kisspeptin important for fertility?
new_faqs.answer: Human genetics shows that its receptor is needed for normal puberty and reproduction: people with loss-of-function mutations in the kisspeptin receptor (GPR54, also called KISS1R) have hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (de Roux et al., PNAS 2003, PMID 12944565; Seminara et al., N Engl J Med 2003, PMID 14573733). In small studies of healthy volunteers, kisspeptin raised LH and FSH (Dhillo et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2005, PMID 16174713). This is why researchers describe it as a key regulator of the reproductive hormone axis. It is not an approved fertility treatment, and no kisspeptin product is FDA-approved.

new_faqs.question: Does repeated kisspeptin exposure cause tachyphylaxis?
new_faqs.answer: In one small randomized trial it did. Women with hypothalamic amenorrhea given repeated kisspeptin-54 injections for two weeks had strong LH and FSH rises on the first day that were significantly reduced by day 14, while they stayed responsive to GnRH (Jayasena et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2009, PMID 19820030; five women per group). The authors described this as desensitization to kisspeptin’s effects on gonadotropin release. The study used kisspeptin-54 in one patient group and does not establish how kisspeptin-10 behaves with repeated exposure. No kisspeptin product is FDA-approved. FDA places kisspeptin-10 in 503A category 2 for significant safety risks, and WADA prohibits kisspeptin and its agonist analogues in males (2026 List, S2.2.1). This page does not give dosing or scheduling guidance.

new_faqs.question: Do effects differ between men and women?
new_faqs.answer: In small human studies, yes. In healthy men, kisspeptin-54 and kisspeptin-10 raised LH (Dhillo et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2005, PMID 16174713; Jayasena et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011, PMID 21976724). In healthy women, kisspeptin-54 raised LH in every menstrual phase tested, most in the preovulatory phase and least in the follicular phase (Dhillo et al. 2007, PMID 17635940); kisspeptin-10 did not change gonadotropins in the follicular phase but raised them in the preovulatory phase (Jayasena et al. 2011). Each study had only a few volunteers per group, so these findings do not establish effects outside those study settings.
